title: Back-pocket brief: contextualization & token-cost tradeoffs
content:
Purpose: jot down rapid takeaways from a few recent reads + quick experiment ideas that I can carry in my back pocket. Not polished — mostly capture intuition, open questions, and cheap tests to try on staging.

TL;DRs (very short):
- "Attention as Indexing" (paper A, arXiv link above): main claim — sparse/keyed attention patterns + small routing reduce compute on long contexts with minimal quality regression for retrieval-augmented tasks. Takeaway: potential to prune KV scans when prefix similarity below threshold; useful for chat history trimming.
- "Progressive KV Compression" (paper B): demonstrates lightweight lossy compression of KV cache (quantized residuals) with graceful degradation. Takeaway: 4–6x memory wins on 8k windows, latency hit small if implemented at kernel level.
- "Prompt Window Economics" (blog-style study): shows cost vs. perf curve for keeping vs. re-embedding conversation history; sweet spot depends on model size and retrieval hit-rate.

Practical heuristics I care about:
- If retrieval hit-rate > 30% and average context reuse > 2 turns, caching prefixes pays off beyond ~10k tokens/week.
- For deterministic chat (system + user + assistant snippets), consider 1) compacting assistant utterances to role tokens + 2) hashing repeated facts into a single short tokenized summary.

Cheap experiments to validate (priority order):
1) KV eviction ablation on staging with 7B quantized model — implement LRU vs. similarity-threshold (cosine < 0.75) evict and record downstream QA F1 + latency. (metrics: avg latency p50/p95, tokens served per-second, QA F1, cost-per-1000-requests)
2) Micro-benchmark residual compression: run 2500 chats, apply 3-bit residual quantization on KV and compare generation quality on 100 eval prompts. (baseline: none)
3) Rolling-window summarization: reduce earlier context to 64-token summary using embedding-cluster pipeline and measure hallucination rate on RAG tasks.

Evaluation prompts (quick set):
- "Given the following user profile and last 6 turns, answer their question without repeating previous assistant steps." (designed to detect missing context)
- Multi-hop retrieval question where answer requires two different earlier messages.
- Safety/regression probe: ask for contradictory instruction buried in early context.

Operational notes / integration thoughts:
- Redwood runtime hooks: where to insert compression? Ideally between KV write and kernel layout; add a flag to call a lightweight compressor in the serving path.
- Rollout: feature gated on Dedicated/Private with metric guardrail RINF-842. Canary on 10% traffic then 50% with automatic rollback on >1.5x p95 latency or >3% drop in eval score.

Open questions / unknowns:
- E2E latency delta when compressor runs on same GPU vs. offloaded to CPU? (need microbenchmarked kernel)
- How often do summaries drift and cause silent failures in multi-turn tasks? Need recall-focused eval.
- Worst-case adversarial sequences that force cache churn — what's upper bound on token generation cost?

To-dos (next week):
- Prototype similarity-threshold eviction on local 7B container (me) — target: lightweight prototype by Tues.
- Create eval set of 120 prompts focusing on retrieval + multi-turn grounding (Lena) — include golden answers and hallucination tags.
- Draft canary rollout doc for RINF-842 (Evan) — include exact metric thresholds and alerting playbook.

Slack refs / quick links:
- #kv-cache-experiments thread (see pinned summary)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache-experiments/pull/271 (proto compressor)

Notes-to-self: keep this intentionally short. If something looks promising, move a cleaned summary to Confluence under "Contextual Cost Playbook" and link the experiment artifacts.

Unresolved: where to store compressed-KV format spec so it can be consumed by private deployments without breaking backward compatibility? Put this on the agenda for infra sync.

Random scribble: "If we can shave 20% token compute by lossy prefix compaction while holding p95 within 10ms, that's an easy product win for Dedicated customers with heavy context workloads."

End.
